newsitem.title: Belarus: Belarus plays down Yeltsin unity offer.
newsitem.headline: Belarus plays down Yeltsin unity offer.

text.p: Belarus's new foreign minister on Tuesday played down Russian President Boris Yeltsin's call to speed up plans to merge the two countries but said his government would move ahead with integrating the two economies.

Ivan Antonovich also dismissed the Council of Europe's suspension of Belarus's guest status on charges that the country had failed to observe democratic norms after a referendum last year boosted the powers of President Alexander Lukashenko.
It was not up to Western countries, he said, to determine Belarus's constitution and laws.

Antonovich, appointed last weekend, told a news conference that Yeltsin's proposal to hold a referendum on unity between the two Slav neighbours was "merely a working document which we believe does not merit any international dimension".
He dismissed suggestions by commentators that the proposal, made while Yeltsin was undergoing hospital treatment for pneumonia, sought to counter NATO's planned eastward expansion.
Both Russia and Belarus oppose the Western alliance's enlargement.
"This is not an answer to the West and it is not made within the context of NATO," he said.
He said Yeltsin had simply set down various tasks -- synchronising economic reforms, customs services and creating a joint energy system.
He had little enthusiasm for Yeltsin's proposed plebiscite. "Perhaps it's time to take a rest from referendums," he said.

Lukashenko, an ardent proponent of reunification since his election in 1994, welcomed Yeltsin's proposal after it was issued on Monday. But Antonovich said the offer was nothing new and amounted to a reply to similar calls by Lukashenko.

The signature last April of a document creating a "community" between the two neighbours has made little progress. At that time, it unleashed a series of large and often violent demonstrations by liberals and nationalists.

Minor scuffles broke out when a few dozen demonstrators gathered on Tuesday outside the Russian embassy in Minsk. But the main nationalist group, the Belarussian Popular Front (BNF), said it had no plans to stage major protests.
Antonovich said the Council of Europe's suspension order showed the West had no understanding of events in Belarus.

"We are not isolated. European leaders simply reacted negatively to our referendum during our constitutional crisis," he said. "Only the Belarussian people, now and in future, can determine by which constitution they want to live."
Belarus is the only European country outside former Yugoslavia still to be admitted to the Council, which oversees the development of democracy and human rights in Europe.
Lukashenko secured greatly expanded powers in last November's referendum and subsequently dissolved parliament, replacing it with a legislature packed with his supporters.

The president has rejected criticism of his authoritarian rule, including a public rebuke in December at a summit of the the more than 50 nations in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
